items.name: category
items.statement_summary: A category consists of objects and arrows; each arrow f has a domain dom(f) and codomain cod(f) (f:A→B). For arrows f:A→B, g:B→C with cod(f)=dom(g) there is a composite g∘f:A→C, and each object A has an identity 1_A:A→A. These satisfy associativity h∘(g∘f)=(h∘g)∘f and unit laws f∘1_A=f=1_B∘f. Objects need not be sets and arrows need not be functions.

items.name: Sets, Sets_fin, and preimage-restricted categories of sets
items.statement_summary: The category Sets of all sets and functions, and Sets_fin of finite sets. Also categories restricting arrows: finite sets with injective functions; and sets with functions whose fibres f^{-1}(b) are all size ≤ 2, all finite, or all infinite.

items.name: categories of structured sets
items.statement_summary: Concrete categories whose objects are structured sets and whose arrows are structure-preserving functions: groups & homomorphisms; vector spaces & linear maps; graphs & graph homomorphisms; ℝ & continuous maps; open subsets of ℝ & continuous maps; topological spaces & continuous maps; manifolds & smooth maps; ℕ & recursive functions; posets & monotone maps.

items.name: poset (partially ordered set) and monotone map
items.statement_summary: A poset is a set A with a relation ≤_A that is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric. An arrow of posets is a monotone function m (a≤a' implies m(a)≤m(a')). Example: ℝ with its usual order.

items.name: Pos, the category of posets and monotone maps
items.statement_summary: Posets and monotone functions form a category Pos: identity functions are monotone and composites of monotone functions are monotone.

items.name: Rel, the category of sets and binary relations
items.statement_summary: Objects are sets; an arrow A→B is a relation R⊆A×B; identity is the diagonal; composition is the relative product S∘R={(a,c)|∃b.(a,b)∈R∧(b,c)∈S}. (Being a category is left as an exercise.) Arrows are not functions.

items.name: category of finite sets and natural-number matrices
items.statement_summary: Objects are finite sets; an arrow A→B is an |A|×|B| matrix of natural numbers; composition is matrix multiplication and identities are identity matrices. Arrows are not functions.

items.name: finite categories 0, 1, 2, 3
items.statement_summary: Small finite categories by objects and generating arrows: 1 (one object, only identity); 2 (two objects, one non-identity arrow); 3 (a→b, b→c, composite a→c); 0 (empty). A finite specification with loops must be cut by equations, e.g. a parallel pair f,g:A⇉B generates infinitely many arrows unless a relation such as gf=1_A is imposed.

items.name: functor
items.statement_summary: A functor F:C→D sends objects to objects and arrows to arrows such that F(f:A→B):F(A)→F(B), F(g∘f)=F(g)∘F(f), and F(1_A)=1_{F(A)}.

items.name: Cat, the category of categories and functors
items.statement_summary: Functors compose associatively and each category C has an identity functor 1_C, so categories and functors form a category Cat.

items.name: preorder
items.statement_summary: A preorder is a set P with a relation ≤ that is reflexive and transitive; antisymmetry is not required.

items.name: a preorder as a category (and the converse)
items.statement_summary: Any preorder (P,≤) is a category with a unique arrow a→b iff a≤b (eq. (1.2)); reflexivity/transitivity give identities/composites. Conversely, any category with at most one arrow between any two objects gives a preorder.

items.name: a poset as a category; power-set poset P(X)
items.statement_summary: A poset is an antisymmetric preorder, hence a thin category. Example: the power set P(X) ordered by inclusion. A functor between poset categories is exactly a monotone function.

items.name: category of a deductive system (proofs as arrows)
items.statement_summary: The category of a deductive system has formulas as objects and deductions/proofs p:φ→ψ as arrows; composition is concatenation of deductions, identities are trivial deductions, and there may be many arrows φ→ψ.

items.name: category C(L) of a functional programming language; denotational semantics functor
items.statement_summary: C(L) has data types as objects and programs as arrows; composition g∘f=f;g, identity is the do-nothing program. Denotational semantics is a functor S:C(L)→D (e.g. D = Scott domains).

items.name: discrete category Dis(X)
items.statement_summary: For a set X, Dis(X) has the elements of X as objects and only identity arrows. Discrete categories are the very special posets having only identity arrows.

items.name: monoid
items.statement_summary: A monoid is a set M with an associative binary operation ·:M×M→M and a unit element u∈M with u·x=x=x·u.

items.name: monoid as a one-object category
items.statement_summary: A monoid is a category with one object: arrows are elements, identity is the unit, composition is the operation. Conversely, for any object C, Hom_C(C,C) is a monoid under composition. A monoid homomorphism corresponds to a functor between one-object categories.

items.name: Mon, the category of monoids and monoid homomorphisms
items.statement_summary: Monoids and monoid homomorphisms form a category Mon. A homomorphism h:M→N preserves the operation h(m·n)=h(m)·h(n) and the unit h(u_M)=u_N.

items.name: isomorphism
items.statement_summary: In a category, f:A→B is an isomorphism if there is g:B→A with g∘f=1_A and f∘g=1_B. The inverse is unique (f^{-1}); A≅B when an isomorphism exists. This can differ from 'bijective homomorphism' (e.g. in Pos).

items.name: group
items.statement_summary: A group is a monoid in which every element has an inverse; equivalently, a one-object category in which every arrow is an isomorphism.

items.name: automorphism group Aut(X); groups of permutations
items.statement_summary: Aut(X) is the group of automorphisms (permutations) of X, i.e. the isomorphisms of X in Sets. A group of permutations is a subgroup G⊆Aut(X): contains 1_X, closed under composition and inverses.

items.name: group homomorphism
items.statement_summary: A homomorphism of groups h:G→H is a homomorphism of the underlying monoids; it necessarily preserves inverses, h(g^{-1})=h(g)^{-1}.

items.name: Cayley's theorem
items.statement_summary: Every group G is isomorphic to a group of permutations. Proof sketch: the Cayley representation Ḡ⊆Aut(G), assigning to g the left-translation ḡ(h)=g·h; the maps i(g)=ḡ and j(ḡ)=g are mutually inverse group homomorphisms.

items.name: Warning: two levels of isomorphism in Cayley's proof
items.statement_summary: Cayley's proof involves two isomorphism notions in different categories: permutations of the underlying set are isomorphisms in Sets, whereas G≅Ḡ lives in Groups. Isomorphism is always relative to an ambient category.

items.name: every category with a set of arrows is isomorphic to a concrete one
items.statement_summary: Every category C whose arrows form a set is isomorphic to a category of sets and functions. Proof sketch (Cayley representation Č): for each object C take Č={f | cod(f)=C}, and for each arrow g:C→D take ḡ:Č→Ḓ, ḡ(f)=g∘f. The set-of-arrows hypothesis is needed so each Č is a set (cf. §1.8).

items.name: what 'concrete category' should mean
items.statement_summary: Since every category is isomorphic to one of sets and functions, the naive 'concrete category' idea is defective. Better: arrows f:C→D are determined by composites with x:T→C from a test object T (fx=gx for all x implies f=g). A category is concrete when this holds for T a terminal object (§2.2), though other T are worth considering.

items.name: product category C×D and projection functors
items.statement_summary: C×D has objects (C,D) and arrows (f,g):(C,D)→(C',D'); composition and identities are componentwise. Projection functors π₁:C×D→C and π₂:C×D→D. For groups G,H the product category is the direct product G×H.

items.name: opposite (dual) category C^op
items.statement_summary: C^op has the same objects as C, and an arrow f:C→D in C^op is an arrow f:D→C in C — arrows are formally reversed. Composition and units in C^op are defined from C by 1_{C̄}=̅{1_C} and f̄∘ḡ=̅{g∘f}. Many duality theorems assert a category is (a subcategory of) the opposite of another (e.g. Sets dual to complete atomic Boolean algebras).

items.name: arrow category C^->
items.statement_summary: C^-> has the arrows of C as objects; a morphism from f:A→B to f':A'→B' is a pair (g1,g2) forming a commutative square g2∘f=f'∘g1. Identity on f is (1_A,1_B), composition is componentwise. Two functors dom, cod: C^-> -> C return domain resp. codomain.

items.name: slice category C/C
items.statement_summary: For an object C, C/C has as objects arrows f with cod(f)=C, and as a morphism from f:X→C to f':X'→C an arrow g:X→X' with f'∘g=f. Forgetful functor U:C/C→C sends each object-arrow to its domain. For a poset P and p, P/p ≅ the principal ideal down(p).

items.name: coslice (under) category C\C
items.statement_summary: C\C has as objects arrows f with dom(f)=C, and as a morphism from f:C→X to f':C→X' an arrow h:X→X' with h∘f=f'. It is the dual of the slice construction, definable as (C^op/C)^op.

items.name: category Sets_* of pointed sets
items.statement_summary: Sets_* has as objects pointed sets (A,a) and as morphisms basepoint-preserving functions f:A→B with f(a)=b. It is isomorphic to the coslice 1\Sets (Sets under a singleton), since functions a:1→A correspond to elements a∈A.

items.name: free monoid A* / M(A) on a set
items.statement_summary: For a set (alphabet) A, the free monoid A* has finite words as elements, concatenation as multiplication, empty word as unit; letters embed via i:A→A*. M(A) is defined by its UMP: for every monoid N and function f:A→|N| there is a unique homomorphism f̄:M(A)→N with |f̄|∘i=f. Consequence: the free monoid on a one-element set ≅ (N,+).

items.name: forgetful functor |-|: Mon -> Sets
items.statement_summary: The forgetful functor sends each monoid N to its underlying set |N| and each homomorphism f to its underlying function |f|, preserving identities and composition; the free monoid's UMP is stated against it.

items.name: (A*, *) has the UMP of the free monoid on A
items.statement_summary: The word monoid (A*,*) satisfies the free-monoid UMP on A: given f:A→|N|, the assignment f̄(a1...ai)=f(a1)*...*f(ai) (empty word ↦ unit) is the unique homomorphism M(A)→N agreeing with f on generators. Proved by constructing f̄ and verifying uniqueness.

items.name: free monoid unique up to isomorphism
items.statement_summary: If M with i:A→|M| and N with j:A→|N| both have the free-monoid UMP on A, there is a unique isomorphism h:M≅N with |h|∘i=j and |h^{-1}|∘j=i. Proof: the two UMPs induce mutually inverse homomorphisms whose composites are identities by uniqueness.

items.name: directed graph
items.statement_summary: A directed graph is a set V of vertices and a set E of edges with two functions s:E→V (source) and t:E→V (target). It is like a category without composition or identity edges.

items.name: free category C(G) on a graph
items.statement_summary: C(G) on a directed graph G has vertices as objects and finite paths (edge sequences e_n...e_1 with t(e_i)=s(e_{i+1})) as arrows; composition is concatenation, identity is the empty path. Special cases: one-vertex graph → free monoid on its edges; edgeless → discrete category; two-parallel-edge graph → infinitely many arrows. UMP: a graph hom i:G→U(C(G)) such that every graph hom h:G→U(D) extends to a unique functor h̄:C(G)→D with U(h̄)∘i=h.

items.name: forgetful functor U: Cat -> Graphs
items.statement_summary: A category is presented by objects C0, arrows C1, composable pairs C2, with dom, cod:C1→C0, i:C0→C1, and composition C2→C1; a functor is a pair (F0,F1) commuting with all these. The forgetful functor U:Cat→Graphs sends a category to its underlying graph C1⇉C0 (keeping dom/cod, discarding identities and composition) and functors to their graph-homomorphism part.

items.name: homomorphism of graphs
items.statement_summary: A graph homomorphism h:G→H is a pair (h0:G0→H0, h1:G1→H1) preserving sources and targets (commuting with s and t) — a 'functor without the identity/composition conditions'. Graphs with these morphisms form the category Graphs.

items.name: small / large category
items.statement_summary: A category C is small if both C0 (objects) and C1 (arrows) are sets; otherwise large. Examples: finite categories and Sets_fin are small; Pos, Groups, Sets are large; Cat (all small categories) is itself large, hence not an object of itself.

items.name: locally small category
items.statement_summary: A category C is locally small if for any objects X,Y the collection Hom_C(X,Y)={f∈C1 : f:X→Y} is a set (a hom-set). Sets is locally small (Hom(X,Y)=Y^X), as are Pos, Top, Group; every small category is locally small.

items.name: Rel is a category
items.statement_summary: Show Rel is a category: objects are sets, an arrow f:A→B is a relation f⊆A×B, identity is the diagonal, composition g∘f={(a,c)|∃b.(a,b)∈f∧(b,c)∈g}.

items.name: isomorphisms of categories (Rel, Sets, powerset poset)
items.statement_summary: Determine which hold: (a) Rel ≅ Rel^op; (b) Sets ≅ Sets^op; (c) for a fixed set X, the poset category P(X) satisfies P(X) ≅ P(X)^op.

items.name: isomorphisms vs bijective homomorphisms
items.statement_summary: Show that (a) in Sets isomorphisms are exactly bijections; (b) in Monoids isomorphisms are exactly bijective homomorphisms; (c) in Posets isomorphisms are NOT the bijective monotone homomorphisms.

items.name: coslice from slice via the opposite construction
items.statement_summary: Construct the coslice category C\C under an object C using the slice construction C/C together with the opposite (-)^op operation.

items.name: free categories on graphs with exactly six arrows
items.statement_summary: Determine how many free categories on graphs have exactly six arrows, and draw the generating graphs.

items.name: prove the UMP for free categories on graphs
items.statement_summary: Prove the UMP of the free category on a graph: given C(G) and i:G→U(C(G)), show that for every category D and graph hom f:G→U(D) there is a unique functor h̄:C(G)→D with U(h̄)∘i=f.
